newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Contradiction? Mao should've seen Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Contradiction? Mao should've seen Hong Kong.

text.p: Chairman Mao used to say his revolutionary movement faced two main "contradictions", but the Great Helmsman never visited Hong Kong, a geo-political oddity that thrives on masses of them.
Capitalist to the backbone against all communist dogma, it's a place like no other on earth and when British rule ends on June 30 it will be an extraordinary corner of China.
Without physical resources -- even the water is piped across the border from China -- Hong Kong's hard work and skill has turned a sweatshop economy into a world-ranked financial centre.
Using dialectical language, Mao proposed that internal Communist Party rifts could be negotiated, but only conflict could settle obstacles between the party and outsiders.
Twenty-one years after his death, the wealthy stockbrokers of Hong Kong avidly collect Mao memorabilia on fortunes built from a "red chip" share-boom in communist mainland enterprises.
Besides stock exchange gambling fever, there's also horse-race betting mania, with an annual turnover equivalent to US$11 billion -- a third of Britain's foreign exchange reserves.
It's all part of a hectic, incessant Hong Kong "buzz" of excitement that starts before you arrive.
COMING IN TO LAND, LIKE "STAR WARS"
Remember those battle scenes in the "Star Wars" movies -- combat planes flying sideways through canyon-blocks of space cities? Coming into Hong Kong is like that.
Airline pilots sometimes announce to passengers: "We are about to make a sharp turn -- this is entirely normal."
You never get used to this moment. Suddenly one wing tips up and beyond it you can see into apartment block windows -- people reading newspapers, having meals. You could almost reach them.
The airport isn't out of town, but right in the middle of this skyscraper city, built on harbourside reclaimed land, partly by British slave labour during Japan's World War Two occupation.

The plane has banked steeply over Kowloon, one of the most densely-inhabited regions on earth. Imagine life there. It's not just the neighbours -- millions of them -- but every two minutes a jet arrives or departs, sideways, past the kitchen window.

You have landed in a place that is hard to classify -- more than a city, less than a nation. It's called a "British colony" but this is misleading. Here is a 98 percent Chinese metropolis, dependent on nobody, run and financed by refugee families from a motherland they rejoin on June 30.

It's cleaner, more modern and more efficient than London, the ancient, grimy capital of its colonial godfather where the biggest share-listed company is the Hong Kong and Shanghai Bank. In terms of shareholder equity, it's the world's biggest bank.
MANDARIN-TYPE CIVIL SERVANTS RUN GOVERNMENT
"The acorn has fallen a hell of a long way from the oak," a British diplomat murmured into his traditional "sundowner", the pink gin drink that has long consoled the empire-builders.

It is run by mandarin-type elite civil servants, rather like the court of the Qing Dynasty which lost Hong Kong in an Opium War with the British in 1841. In fact there are two governments -- one waiting to take over from July 1.
Britain at first didn't even want this "barren rock" and sent the man who claimed it for Queen Victoria was sent as envoy to the then Republic of Texas, seen as equivalent to Siberia.

In contrast to economic freedom, there's a bossy atmosphere that doesn't always make sense. "Stand on the right" say escalator signs at the underground railway. "Walk on the left" say signs at the stairs. Some bilingual street signs say different things in English and Chinese.
Top bureaucrats reflect a British civil service based on the Celestial Empire's Mandarin system of administration.

There's no elected cabinet. So there are no votes to be wooed by the executive policy-makers, all civil servants, but they regularly notch up hefty budget surpluses that most Western finance ministers would die for.
No-one seems particularly grateful. In a place awash with money -- $US25,000 average income is among the world's highest -- the newspapers complain: "Another boring budget surplus!"
Turn-of-century doubledecker tramcars still trundle along and ancient passenger-ferries criss-cross the great harbour.
Nearly everything else is state-of-art as the world's seventh-largest trading economy grows daily in a once-sleepy backwater of the old Chinese Empire.
"If he had come from Hong Kong," said the diplomat, "Chairman Mao might have said power grows out of a chequebook, not the barrel of a gun."
